title: From Auteuil to the Cork-Lined Room: Proust, the Salons, and the Recovery of Combray
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Auteuil, birth in the great-uncle's house
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In the house of his great-uncle Louis Weil at Auteuil, west of the old city wall, Jeanne Clemence Weil gives birth to a first son two months after the Commune falls. The family had left central Paris for the suburb to sit out the siege and the killing that followed it. The father, Adrien Proust, is a physician who will spend his career building the quarantine cordon that keeps cholera out of western Europe; the mother comes of a prosperous Jewish family. The child is frail in the first hour and is not expected to live the week.
suggested_refs: The Weil house at Auteuil, rue La Fontaine, birthplace and one of the models scholars assign to Combray
sources: Jean-Yves Tadie, Marcel Proust: A Life

stops.name: Eglise Saint-Louis-d'Antin, the baptism
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Four weeks old, the boy is carried into Saint-Louis-d'Antin on the rue de Caumartin and baptized into his father's Catholicism. His mother never converts. Marcel grows up inside that division without ever resolving it, an unbelieving Catholic with a Jewish mother, and the Dreyfus years will turn the arrangement into a public question he cannot decline to answer. The church still stands behind the department stores of the ninth arrondissement, a working parish on a street of shopfronts.
suggested_refs: The baptismal register of Saint-Louis-d'Antin, 5 August 1871

stops.name: Illiers, the house of aunt Elisabeth Amiot
stops.date_confidence: traditional: repeated Easter and summer visits across the later 1870s; no single visit is documented to a date
stops.campa: At Easter the boy is sent down to Illiers in the Eure-et-Loir, to the house of his aunt Elisabeth Amiot: a garden, a staircase, a bedroom above the street, an aunt keeping to her bed and her tisane and the town's business. He will take the measurements of this house and set them down as Combray. What happens here in the fiction, the crumb of cake in the spoonful of tea, is a scene from the novel and not a documented afternoon; in Proust's own earlier draft the trigger is dry toast. The house is now the Musee Marcel Proust.
stops.quote: She sent out for one of those short, plump little cakes called 'petites madeleines,' which look as though they had been moulded in the fluted scallop of a pilgrim's shell. And soon, mechanically, weary after a dull day with the prospect of a depressing morrow, I raised to my lips a spoonful of the tea in which I had soaked a morsel of the cake. No sooner had the warm liquid, and the crumbs with it, touched my palate than a shudder ran through my whole body... I had ceased now to feel mediocre, accidental, mortal.
stops.quote_source: Swann's Way (In Search of Lost Time, Vol. 1), Overture, trans. C. K. Scott Moncrieff (1922); en.wikisource.org. Ellipsis marks an internal cut in a longer verified paragraph.
suggested_refs: The Maison de tante Leonie, rue du Docteur Proust, Illiers-Combray, now the Musee Marcel Proust
Contre Sainte-Beuve, in which the memory trigger is dry toast rather than a madeleine

stops.name: Illiers, the church of Saint-Jacques
stops.date_confidence: traditional: no attendance at this church on any given date is documented; the identification with Saint-Hilaire is the town's
stops.campa: The parish church of Illiers carries a single spire visible from every lane of the town and from the fields beyond it. Illiers holds, and has held for a century, that this is the church of Saint-Hilaire that occupies the opening pages of the novel: the spire seen from the train, the tapestries, the dark saint in the window. Proust never said so. The identification belongs to the town rather than to the author, and the town has since staked everything on it, down to the name it now bears.
suggested_refs: The church of Saint-Jacques at Illiers-Combray and the local tradition identifying it with Saint-Hilaire

stops.name: 9 boulevard Malesherbes, the asthmatic child
stops.date_confidence: year approximate: the first attack is placed 'around age nine' in the sources; no day or month attested
stops.campa: The family has an apartment on boulevard Malesherbes, and here the child who cannot sleep until his mother has come upstairs to kiss him goodnight becomes, at about nine, an asthmatic. The first attack is severe enough that Adrien Proust, the hygienist, thinks his son may die in the room with him. From that morning Marcel is an invalid by profession: fumigations, closed windows, dust-free rooms, a lifetime itinerary of cures. He spends the next forty-two years arranging a life around a set of lungs.
suggested_refs: The Proust family apartment at 9 boulevard Malesherbes, 75008 Paris

stops.name: Lycee Condorcet, the first reviews
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of entry; the term start is conventional
stops.campa: At eleven he enters the lycee on the rue du Havre, and his schooling proceeds in fits: whole terms lost to asthma, prizes taken in French composition. He finds there the friends who become his adult circle, and with them founds the small reviews that print his earliest prose, a society column in Le Mensuel in 1890 and the literary Le Banquet in 1892. Each magazine folds inside a year or two. The habit of writing for a circle of intimates who will read every line does not fold with them.
suggested_refs: Runs of Le Mensuel (1890) and Le Banquet (1892), Proust's first appearances in print

stops.name: Orleans, the year at the Coligny barracks
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of service, 1889 to 1890; the month is conventional
stops.campa: He volunteers for a single year with the 76th infantry regiment at the Coligny barracks in Orleans, taking the one-year term the law still allows. He rides badly, freezes, finishes near the bottom of his class, and afterwards remembers the year as one of the happiest of his life. The regiment remembers a courteous, odd, unwell recruit whose mother came to visit. Doncieres, the garrison town where the narrator goes to stay with Saint-Loup, is built out of these months and out of nothing else.
suggested_refs: The Coligny barracks, faubourg Bannier, Orleans, quarters of the 76th infantry regiment

stops.name: Paris, the drawing room of Madame Straus
stops.date_confidence: range: he is received from the early 1890s onward; no first visit is dated in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Genevieve Halevy, widow of Georges Bizet and now Mme Emile Straus, is the mother of his schoolfriend and keeps the wittiest drawing room in Paris. Proust is admitted at twenty and stays admitted. What he learns here is listening, the one activity he will later be accused of practising to the exclusion of every other. Her phrasing, her migraines, her trick of undoing a compliment with the second half of the sentence: it goes down at the time and comes back out, twenty years later, as the Duchesse de Guermantes.
suggested_refs: The correspondence of Marcel Proust and Genevieve Straus, spanning thirty years

stops.name: Rue d'Astorg, the salon of the comtesse Greffulhe
stops.date_confidence: range: the 1890s into the 1900s; no single reception is dated in the sources consulted
stops.campa: In the townhouse on the rue d'Astorg the comtesse Elisabeth Greffulhe receives, and is looked at. She is the most photographed beauty in Paris and the cousin of Robert de Montesquiou, who brings Proust in. She is also unapproachable by design, and that is the quality he studies hardest. Her bearing goes into the Duchesse de Guermantes alongside Mme Straus's tongue. Montesquiou himself, the aesthete with the cane and the cruelty, will be taken apart and rebuilt across four volumes as the Baron de Charlus.
suggested_refs: The Greffulhe collection of photographs and gowns, Palais Galliera, Paris

stops.name: Chateau de Reveillon, the summer with Reynaldo Hahn
stops.date_confidence: attested for the summers of 1894 and 1895; the day is conventional
stops.campa: Madeleine Lemaire, the watercolourist whose roses sell better than her portraits, keeps a country house near Sezanne and fills it each August with musicians and painters. Proust comes down with Reynaldo Hahn, twenty years old, Venezuelan-born, already a composer, and the two of them spend the summer in a companionship the household does not pretend not to see. Lemaire will illustrate his first book, Les plaisirs et les jours, which appears in 1896 with a preface by Anatole France and sells almost nothing. Hahn outlasts everyone.
suggested_refs: Les plaisirs et les jours (Calmann-Levy, 1896), illustrated by Madeleine Lemaire, preface by Anatole France

segments.name: The Degrees, the Library, and the Duel

stops.name: The Sorbonne, the licence in philosophy
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of March 1895; the day is not established in the sources consulted
stops.campa: He takes the licence es lettres in philosophy in March, the degree he actually finishes. Behind him lie a licence en droit and several years at the Ecole libre des sciences politiques, which he leaves in 1890 from the diplomatic section without a diploma. His father wants a profession for him and will go on wanting one; Marcel practises neither law nor diplomacy for a day. What survives from the philosophy is a single proposition the novel will spend three thousand pages demonstrating.
stops.quote: It is a labour in vain to attempt to recapture it: all the efforts of our intellect must prove futile. The past is hidden somewhere outside the realm, beyond the reach of intellect, in some material object (in the sensation which that material object will give us) which we do not suspect. And as for that object, it depends on chance whether we come upon it or not before we ourselves must die.
stops.quote_source: Swann's Way (In Search of Lost Time, Vol. 1), Overture, trans. C. K. Scott Moncrieff (1922); en.wikisource.org
suggested_refs: The Sorbonne records of the licence es lettres, March 1895
The Ecole libre des sciences politiques register showing his departure in 1890 without a diploma
sources: proust-ink.com biography (which misdates the degrees; see report)

stops.name: Bibliotheque Mazarine, the post never worked
stops.date_confidence: attested: the librarian's examination was sat 29 June 1895
stops.campa: He sits the librarian's examination on the twenty-ninth of June and is placed as an unsalaried attache at the Mazarine, under the dome on the quai de Conti. He appears there, on and off, for about four months. Then he asks for leave, and the leave is extended, and extended again, until the post lapses around 1900. The story that he never once set foot in the library is repeated everywhere and is not true. What is true is that a professional life was arranged on paper and never lived, and that his father had wanted one.
suggested_refs: The Bibliotheque Mazarine personnel records for the unsalaried attache of 1895
sources: Wikipedia, 'Marcel Proust' (which gives 1896 and the 'never worked' claim; see report)

stops.name: Dieppe, the house on the Channel
stops.date_confidence: attested to August 1895; the day is conventional
stops.campa: Proust and Hahn take a house together on the Channel at Dieppe, the one stretch of the friendship that biographers describe as settled and open rather than a passion managed at a distance. It is a working holiday. Between the beach and the casino he begins accumulating the pages of a novel about a young man named Jean Santeuil, which will run to a thousand sheets and never find its shape. The Channel here is grey and shallow and disappoints him. Within weeks the two of them go looking for the Atlantic.
suggested_refs: The Proust-Hahn correspondence of the summer of 1895
sources: William Carter, Marcel Proust: A Life

stops.name: Beg-Meil, the first novel begun and abandoned
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1895; the day is conventional
stops.campa: At a fishing village in Finistere, apple trees running down almost to the water, Proust settles in and writes. The pages are Jean Santeuil: a third-person novel about a young man of his own class and temperament, in which the material of the later book is entirely present and none of it has found its form, because the man doing the remembering is not yet the man telling the story. He works at it four years and stops. It is published in 1952, thirty years after his death, out of a box of loose sheets.
suggested_refs: Jean Santeuil, published posthumously by Gallimard in 1952

stops.name: Bois de Meudon, the duel with Jean Lorrain
stops.date_confidence: attested: 6 February 1897
stops.campa: Jean Lorrain, a journalist who writes about other people's private arrangements for a living, insinuates in print that Proust's connection with Lucien Daudet is what it is. On the sixth of February the two men meet with pistols in the woods at Meudon, outside the city. Shots are exchanged, nobody is hit, and that is the ordinary outcome and rather the point. Proust is twenty-five, asthmatic, and held by everyone who knows him to be incapable of rising before noon. He arrives on time and stands still.
suggested_refs: The Paris press accounts of the Proust-Lorrain duel, February 1897
sources: Wikipedia, 'Marcel Proust' (which places the duel in Paris; see report)

stops.name: Paris, the petition of the intellectuals
stops.date_confidence: range: Zola's J'accuse appeared 13 January 1898 and the petition ran over the following days; Proust's exact signature date is not established here
stops.campa: Zola publishes J'accuse and the petition of the intellectuals follows within days. Proust signs, and by his own later account collected signatures for it, Anatole France's among them. The son of a Catholic hygienist and a Jewish mother is now on a list, and the salons he has spent seven years entering are dividing along the same line. He will go on defending Dreyfus in letters for years after the case is legally closed, long after most of the salons that argued over it have moved on to other quarrels.
suggested_refs: The Manifeste des intellectuels, L'Aurore, January 1898
sources: lionel_royer.journey.json (stop 'Paris, Dreyfus drawn in his cell', 1895-01-20)
Proust's Dreyfusard activity is outside-corpus and reconstructed; see report

segments.name: Ruskin: Evian, Venice, Padua, the Low Countries

stops.name: Evian-les-Bains, the cure at the Hotel Splendide
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1899; the day is conventional
stops.campa: He takes the waters at Evian on the south shore of Lake Geneva, one in a series of cures against asthma and nerves that never work and are never abandoned. The Splendide is a grand hotel of the sort he will spend his life inside and describe with more attention than he ever gives a private house: the corridor, the lift, the dining room glazed along one wall, the staff watched as closely as the guests. Almost nothing of Switzerland reaches the novel. The hotel does, moved to the Norman coast and renamed.
suggested_refs: The Hotel Splendide at Evian-les-Bains and the Proust letters written from it

stops.name: Venice, the Danieli and the Ruskin translation
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1900; the day is conventional
stops.campa: He goes to Venice with his mother and they lodge at the Danieli on the Riva degli Schiavoni. Mornings he works at Ruskin with The Stones of Venice open in front of him, on the marble floor of Saint Mark's when the passage requires it; evenings he watches the light go off the lagoon. His English is poor. The translations are a household manufacture, roughed out by his mother, revised by him, checked by Marie Nordlinger, polished again by him. I do not claim to know English, he says. I claim to know Ruskin.
suggested_refs: John Ruskin, The Stones of Venice, the working text of the 1900 journey
sources: Wikipedia, 'Marcel Proust' (on the group translation and the 'imperfect command of English')

stops.name: Padua, Giotto in the Arena chapel
stops.date_confidence: attested as an excursion within the May 1900 Italian journey; the day is conventional
stops.campa: An excursion inland from Venice to the Arena chapel, where Giotto's Vices and Virtues stand in two ranks along the walls, each allegory labelled and unmistakable, Charity holding out her heart with no expression at all on her face. Readers find this chapel again in the kitchen maid at Combray whom Swann nicknames Giotto's Charity, pregnant and indifferent and carrying the asparagus. That link is critical inference and not a thing Proust set down. What is documented is that he stood here in May 1900.
suggested_refs: Giotto's Vices and Virtues cycle, Cappella degli Scrovegni, Padua

stops.name: The Hague, the patch of yellow wall
stops.date_confidence: attested to the October 1902 journey through Belgium and Holland; the day is conventional
stops.campa: On a Ruskinian tour of Belgium and Holland, made with Bertrand de Fenelon, he comes to the Mauritshuis and stands in front of Vermeer's View of Delft. He fixes on a small patch of yellow wall at the right of the canvas. Twenty years later the writer Bergotte, dying in a gallery of an intestinal attack, will look at that same patch, understand that his own sentences should have been laid on like that, and fall dead on a circular settee. Proust revises the scene on nearly the last working day of his life.
suggested_refs: Vermeer, View of Delft, Mauritshuis, The Hague
sources: fr.wikipedia.org, 'Marcel Proust' (on the 1902 journey with Fenelon)

segments.name: The Parents Die, the Cork Goes Up

stops.name: 45 rue de Courcelles, the father dies
stops.date_confidence: month attested; the day is not established in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Adrien Proust dies in November at the family apartment on the rue de Courcelles. He is a professor of hygiene and an inspector-general of sanitary services, the physician who built the quarantine cordon that kept cholera out of western Europe, and he has spent thirty years waiting for his elder son to take up a profession. Robert Proust, the younger son, has married that same year and moved out. Marcel is thirty-two, unemployed, the author of one thin book and some translations, and living with his mother.
suggested_refs: The Proust apartment at 45 rue de Courcelles, 75008 Paris, occupied 1900 to 1906

stops.name: Paris, La Bible d'Amiens goes to press
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1904; the month and day are conventional
stops.campa: The Ruskin translation appears with a long preface of his own. It is a family manufacture: his mother produces the crib, he works it over, Marie Nordlinger checks it against the English, he polishes it again. Ruskin is the door through which he learns to look at a cathedral, and through which he will keep translating for two more years before the debt to his teacher is paid off in print. He will later say he did not know a word of English when he began; his mother's crib and Nordlinger's checking are the whole of his qualification for the work.
suggested_refs: John Ruskin, La Bible d'Amiens, trans. Marcel Proust (Mercure de France, 1904)
Sesame et les lys, trans. Proust (1906), with his preface Sur la lecture
sources: william_morris.journey.json (stop 'The Nature of Gothic, Ruskin read at Oxford')

stops.name: 45 rue de Courcelles, the mother dies
stops.date_confidence: month attested; the day is not established in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Jeanne Proust dies in September. Her son is thirty-four. She leaves him money enough that he will never need the profession his father wanted, and she takes away with her the only arrangement under which he has so far been able to live at all; he says so himself, repeatedly, for the rest of his life. He wears mourning for the remaining seventeen years. The three years after her death produce almost nothing. Then, in 1908, the writing begins and does not stop until he is dead.
stops.quote: But when from a long-distant past nothing subsists, after the people are dead, after the things are broken and scattered, still, alone, more fragile, but with more vitality, more unsubstantial, more persistent, more faithful, the smell and taste of things remain poised a long time, like souls, ready to remind us, waiting and hoping for their moment, amid the ruins of all the rest; and bear unfaltering, in the tiny and almost impalpable drop of their essence, the vast structure of recollection.
stops.quote_source: Swann's Way (In Search of Lost Time, Vol. 1), Overture, trans. C. K. Scott Moncrieff (1922); en.wikisource.org
suggested_refs: The 1908 Contre Sainte-Beuve notebooks, first drafts feeding directly into the novel

stops.name: Versailles, five months at the Hotel des Reservoirs
stops.date_confidence: attested: August to December 1906
stops.campa: Unable to go back into the apartment where his mother died, and not yet able to take the rooms his great-uncle's estate has made available, he moves to the Hotel des Reservoirs at Versailles and stays five months. He does not go out to look at the palace. He writes to Rene Peter almost daily from a shuttered room a few hundred metres from it. A tradition that puts this stay in September 1914, a flight from German bombardment, has the year and the reason both wrong. In September 1914 he was at Cabourg.
suggested_refs: The Proust letters to Rene Peter from the Hotel des Reservoirs, autumn 1906

stops.name: 102 boulevard Haussmann, the cork-lined room
stops.date_confidence: attested: he moved in on 27 December 1906
stops.campa: He moves in on the twenty-seventh of December, to rooms in a building his great-uncle Louis Weil had occupied and his mother had known. The bedroom walls are lined with cork against noise and pollen. He closes the shutters, sleeps by day, wakes toward evening, takes coffee, and writes through the night in bed with the manuscript on his knees; he calls himself an owl. He keeps this room thirteen years and produces in it the greater part of a novel that opens with a man lying in the dark, not knowing where he is.
stops.quote: For a long time I used to go to bed early. Sometimes, when I had put out my candle, my eyes would close so quickly that I had not even time to say 'I'm going to sleep.'
stops.quote_source: Swann's Way (In Search of Lost Time, Vol. 1), opening sentence, trans. C. K. Scott Moncrieff (1922); Project Gutenberg ebook 7178
suggested_refs: The reconstructed cork-lined bedroom, Musee Carnavalet, Paris

stops.name: Cabourg, the Grand Hotel becomes Balbec
stops.date_confidence: attested: every summer from 1907 until 1914; the day is conventional
stops.campa: Every August from now until the war he takes rooms at the Grand Hotel on the sea front at Cabourg, arriving by hired car and keeping hotel hours that are nobody else's. The long dining room with its wall of glass, the lift boy, the manager's mangled vocabulary, the band of girls along the front: he transposes the building almost without alteration and calls it the Grand-Hotel de Balbec. He is thirty-six and the book has begun. The promenade outside the hotel now carries his name.
suggested_refs: The Grand Hotel de Cabourg, Promenade Marcel Proust

stops.name: Paris, Montesquiou crowns d'Annunzio
stops.date_confidence: attested for d'Annunzio's Paris debut; Proust's presence in the room is not established
stops.campa: Robert de Montesquiou, the model Proust is at this moment dismantling into the Baron de Charlus, presents Gabriele d'Annunzio to Parisian society in March. The Italian arrives a debtor and is crowned within the season. The salons receiving him are the same rooms Proust is writing down in a form the sitters will spend a decade denying and recognizing at once. Nothing establishes that Proust was present. Montesquiou is the hinge, and Montesquiou is in both rooms on the same evenings.
suggested_refs: Robert de Montesquiou's Paris salon in 1910, the crossing point of two atlas travelers
sources: dannunzio.journey.json (stop 'Paris, the exile arrives and is crowned', 1910-03-28)
Tadie, Marcel Proust: A Life (Montesquiou as Charlus model)

stops.name: 102 boulevard Haussmann, Alfred Agostinelli
stops.date_confidence: range: Agostinelli enters the household during 1913 and dies in May 1914; the day is conventional
stops.campa: Alfred Agostinelli, who had driven Proust around Normandy in 1907 as a hired chauffeur, comes back in 1913 and moves into the apartment as secretary. He types. He also wants to fly. In the spring of 1914 he leaves, enrols at a flying school on the Mediterranean under the name Marcel Swann, and drowns when his monoplane goes into the sea off Antibes. Readers have put him inside Albertine ever since. That reading is a tradition, well founded and undocumented, and Proust never confirmed it.
suggested_refs: The Albertine volumes, La Prisonniere and Albertine disparue, and the Agostinelli tradition
sources: Wikipedia, 'Marcel Proust' (relationship attested; the literary link is critical tradition)

stops.name: Theatre des Champs-Elysees, the Rite of Spring
stops.date_confidence: attested for the premiere; Proust's attendance is widely reported tradition and is not documented here
stops.campa: The Rite of Spring is given on the twenty-ninth of May and the house comes apart. Proust is reported in the audience, a report repeated for a century and never established. He is certainly inside the Ballets Russes orbit in these years, dining with dancers and patrons and gossiping about Diaghilev's productions in the same salons he has spent two decades cultivating. The scandal is still being argued over the following year, when Swann's Way finally appears.
stops.quote: But to-night, at Mme. Verdurin's, scarcely had the little pianist begun to play when, suddenly, after a high note held on through two whole bars, Swann saw it approaching, stealing forth from underneath that resonance, which was prolonged and stretched out over it, like a curtain of sound, to veil the mystery of its birth--and recognised, secret, whispering, articulate, the airy and fragrant phrase that he had loved.
stops.quote_source: Swann's Way (In Search of Lost Time, Vol. 1), Swann in Love, trans. C. K. Scott Moncrieff (1922); Project Gutenberg ebook 7178, line 8447, quoted in full
suggested_refs: The Theatre des Champs-Elysees, avenue Montaigne, hall of the 1913 premiere and of Gurdjieff's 1923 demonstrations
sources: gurdjieff.journey.json (December 1923 demonstrations, 'the hall of the Rite of Spring scandal')
isadora_duncan.journey.json (Diaghilev and the Ballets Russes circle)

stops.name: Editions Grasset, Swann's Way at the author's expense
stops.date_confidence: attested: published November 1913
stops.campa: Fasquelle turns the manuscript down. Ollendorff turns it down. At the Nouvelle Revue Francaise, Andre Gide reads a few pages, finds duchesses and syntax he dislikes, and turns it down without reading further. So Proust pays Bernard Grasset to print it: Du cote de chez Swann, at the author's expense, in November. He is forty-two. The reviews are few and the sales slow. Two months later Gide writes him a letter that will be quoted against Gide for the rest of the century.
stops.quote: For several days I have been unable to put your book down... The rejection of this book will remain the most serious mistake ever made by the NRF and, since I bear the shame of being very much responsible for it, one of the most stinging and remorseful regrets of my life.
stops.quote_source: Andre Gide, letter to Marcel Proust, January 1914, with ellipsis in the source; quoted in Tadie, Marcel Proust, p. 611, seen via Wikipedia, 'In Search of Lost Time'
suggested_refs: Du cote de chez Swann (Grasset, 1913), first edition at the author's expense

stops.name: Cabourg, the last summer
stops.date_confidence: attested: he was at Cabourg in September 1914; the day is conventional
stops.campa: The war begins and he goes to Cabourg in September, as he has every year since 1907, and this is the last time. He is forty-three and exempt, and he will spend the war in Paris. The book doubles in size while it waits for a publisher able to print it. The two-volume novel Grasset announced in 1913 becomes the seven volumes that exist, because the war took his readers away for six years and left him nothing to do with the time except go on writing into it.
suggested_refs: The wartime expansion of the manuscript between 1914 and 1918

stops.name: Paris, the raid on Le Cuziat's house
stops.date_confidence: attested: 11 January 1918
stops.campa: The police raid a male brothel kept by Albert Le Cuziat, a former hotel footman, and the register of customers taken that night names Marcel Proust. He is forty-six and the most private man in Paris, and by every account he went there to watch and to listen rather than for anything else. Jupien's establishment in the last volumes is built on these premises. In the novel it is the narrator who stands at the spyhole, and the narrator, alone among the hundreds of named people in the book, has no surname.
stops.quote: one can say anything so long as one does not say 'I.'
stops.quote_source: Marcel Proust to Andre Gide, quoted in Michael Lucey, 'Proust's Queer Metalapses', in Never Say I (Duke University Press, 2006), p. 218; seen via Wikipedia, 'In Search of Lost Time'. Date of the remark unestablished.
suggested_refs: Sodome et Gomorrhe and the Jupien establishment of Le Temps retrouve

segments.name: The Goncourt and the Last Rooms

stops.name: 8bis rue Laurent-Pichat, put out of the cork
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1919; the day is conventional
stops.campa: The building on boulevard Haussmann is sold to a bank and he is put out of the cork-lined room after thirteen years. He lodges in a flat near the Bois de Boulogne belonging to the actress Rejane, with a singer practising overhead and no cork anywhere in the place. He is ill, he cannot work, and the manuscript is in boxes on the floor. Two volumes are in proof while he is in this state. He stays five months and calls the arrangement unlivable in every letter he sends out of it.
suggested_refs: The Proust letters of summer 1919 from the rue Laurent-Pichat

stops.name: 44 rue Hamelin, the last address
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1919; the day is conventional
stops.campa: In October he takes a fifth-floor flat in the rue Hamelin, in Chaillot, and calls it temporary. It is small, dark, badly heated, and he lives in it three years and dies in it. The bedroom is the whole of his territory: the bed, the notebooks, the tisane, the fumigation powder, the manuscript in its paperoles, strips of paper pinned and pasted into the cahiers until some pages open out a metre long. Celeste Albaret keeps the door. He is scarcely seen by daylight again.
suggested_refs: The paperole notebooks of the last years, Bibliotheque nationale de France
Celeste Albaret, Monsieur Proust (1973)

stops.name: Editions Gallimard, the Prix Goncourt
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1919; the day is conventional
stops.campa: Gallimard, having refused Swann six years earlier, buys the whole novel and brings out A l'ombre des jeunes filles en fleurs. In December the Academie Goncourt gives it the prize over Roland Dorgeles's war novel, and the press is furious: the prize has gone to a rich invalid of forty-eight who writes about duchesses, in a year when it ought to have gone to a soldier. The row sells the book. Proust becomes famous in the three years he has left, and the translations begin while he is alive to see them.
suggested_refs: A l'ombre des jeunes filles en fleurs (Gallimard, 1919), Prix Goncourt 1919

stops.name: Place Vendome, the Ritz at impossible hours
stops.date_confidence: range: the Ritz habit runs through the late 1910s and early 1920s; no single evening is dated here
stops.campa: He arrives at the Ritz at hours when nobody else is dining, orders little, tips beyond reason, and keeps the waiters standing at his table answering questions about who came in with whom and what was said. Olivier, the maitre d'hotel, supplies him with the movements of half the Faubourg Saint-Germain. It is field research conducted at night by a man who cannot go out in the day. The hotel is the last public room he uses, and he pays for the privilege at a rate the staff remember for decades.
suggested_refs: The Ritz Paris staff recollections of Proust's late suppers

stops.name: Paris, Gurdjieff arrives four months before the end
stops.date_confidence: attested in the atlas record for Gurdjieff: 14 July 1922; the two men never met
stops.campa: Four months and four days from this date, Proust dies in the cork-lined room at 44 rue Hamelin, correcting the death of a writer, still finishing three thousand pages on what the involuntary memory hands back. He works to the edge of his strength on proofs he insists on checking himself, revising sentences from a bed he can no longer safely leave, adding a death scene to his own manuscript days before his own. The room closes, like the pages, on his own schedule and no one else's.
suggested_refs: The Institute for the Harmonious Development of Man, founded at the Prieure d'Avon in October 1922
sources: gurdjieff.journey.json (stop 'Paris, arrival with the last of the fortune', 1922-07-14)

segments.name: The Death and the Long Afterward

stops.name: 44 rue Hamelin, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested: 18 November 1922
stops.campa: He dies on the eighteenth of November at fifty-one, in the bedroom on the rue Hamelin, of pneumonia and a pulmonary abscess. He had refused to be moved and refused most of what his brother the surgeon prescribed. In the last weeks he was dictating to Celeste Albaret at night and adding to the death of Bergotte, so that a dying writer's final corrections went into a passage about a writer dying. Sources differ on the chain of illness; one account gives pneumonia following untreated bronchitis and asthma. Two days later Man Ray photographs the face at Jean Cocteau's request.
stops.quote: I feel that there is much to be said for the Celtic belief that the souls of those whom we have lost are held captive in some inferior being, in an animal, in a plant, in some inanimate object, and so effectively lost to us until the day (which to many never comes) when we happen to pass by the tree or to obtain possession of the object which forms their prison. Then they start and tremble, they call us by our name, and as soon as we have recognised their voice the spell is broken.
stops.quote_source: Swann's Way (In Search of Lost Time, Vol. 1), Overture, trans. C. K. Scott Moncrieff (1922); en.wikisource.org
suggested_refs: Man Ray's deathbed photograph of Proust, 20 November 1922, commissioned by Jean Cocteau
sources: fr.wikipedia.org, 'Marcel Proust' (Man Ray photograph dated 20 November)

stops.name: Eglise Saint-Pierre-de-Chaillot, the funeral
stops.date_confidence: attested: 21 November 1922, three days after the death; several accounts give 22 November and four days, and are wrong
stops.campa: The funeral is held on the twenty-first at Saint-Pierre-de-Chaillot, a few streets from the room where he died, with military honours for the volunteer of the 76th infantry who served his year at Orleans in 1889. Cocteau is among the mourners. The Man Ray photograph taken the day before, bearded, the face gone very thin against the pillow, is the image the twentieth century keeps and reprints. Three of the seven volumes are still unpublished on the morning of the service.
suggested_refs: The church of Saint-Pierre-de-Chaillot, avenue Marceau, Paris

stops.name: Pere-Lachaise, division 85
stops.date_confidence: attested: burial 21 November 1922, division 85, family vault
stops.campa: He is laid in the family vault in division eighty-five, beside Adrien and Jeanne Proust. The stone is black granite and low to the ground. Visitors leave metro tickets on it, and madeleines, and pencils; the cemetery clears them away and they come back within the week. The novel is complete in draft and not yet in print, and his brother Robert, the surgeon, will spend the next five years getting the last three volumes out of the notebooks and into type.
suggested_refs: The Proust family vault, division 85, cimetiere du Pere-Lachaise

stops.name: Corsica, Oppenheimer reads by flashlight
stops.date_confidence: attested in the atlas record for Robert Oppenheimer: April 1926
stops.campa: Four years after the funeral a twenty-two-year-old physicist, wrecked by depression and close to killing himself, walks Corsica with two friends and reads A la recherche du temps perdu at night by flashlight. Robert Oppenheimer comes off the island able to work again, and lists Proust's novel among his suggested references for the rest of his life. It is one of the plainest tributes his afterlife has left: a book credited, in so many words, with holding a man to his work across four years and a thousand kilometres.
suggested_refs: Robert Oppenheimer's Corsica trip of spring 1926 and his citation of Proust among suggested references
sources: robert_oppenheimer.journey.json (stop 'Corsica: the island that lifted the darkness', 1926-04-01)

stops.name: Editions Gallimard, Le Temps retrouve
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1927; the month and day are conventional
stops.campa: La Prisonniere in 1923, Albertine disparue in 1925, Le Temps retrouve in 1927: the last three volumes are brought out of the notebooks by Robert Proust and published after the author's death, closing a book begun in 1908. In English, C. K. Scott Moncrieff renders six volumes between 1922 and 1930 under a title lifted from Shakespeare, Remembrance of Things Past, and then dies. Stephen Hudson finishes the seventh as Time Regained in 1931. A Penguin team of seven translators, under the general editorship of Christopher Prendergast, does the whole novel again between 1995 and 2002.
stops.quote: Oh if I could write like that!
stops.quote_source: Virginia Woolf, 1922, in The Letters of Virginia Woolf, eds. Nicolson and Trautmann (Harcourt, 1976-77), 2:525; seen via Wikipedia, 'In Search of Lost Time'
suggested_refs: The Scott Moncrieff translation, 1922-1930, completed by Stephen Hudson in 1931
The Penguin translation, general editor Christopher Prendergast, seven translators, 1995-2002

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Recherche reaches the River Plate
stops.date_confidence: range: Sur's Proustian decade runs through the 1930s and 1940s; no single date is fixed here and the link is reconstruction
stops.campa: On the far side of the Atlantic the magazine Sur, founded by Victoria Ocampo, becomes one of the principal Spanish-language channels for Proust in the River Plate. Her sister Silvina Ocampo will edit, in 1940, an anthology of fantastic tales putting Kafka and Chesterton and Cocteau between one set of covers, and Cocteau had stood in the rue Hamelin in November 1922 asking Man Ray to take the photograph. The line runs through a magazine and a translation.
suggested_refs: Sur (Buenos Aires, from 1931) and its Proust translations and criticism
sources: The Sur-Proust connection is outside-corpus reconstruction; see report

stops.name: Illiers-Combray, the town takes the novel's name
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1971, the centenary of his birth; the month and day are conventional
stops.campa: On the centenary of his birth the town of Illiers votes to add the name of the place he invented and becomes Illiers-Combray, the only commune in France named after a fiction. The aunt's house on what is now the rue du Docteur Proust is the Musee Marcel Proust. Scholars point out that Combray was assembled from more than one place, the Auteuil house among them, so the town's claim is a simplification. The town has heard the objection and has kept the name.
stops.quote: The places that we have known belong now only to the little world of space on which we map them for our own convenience. None of them was ever more than a thin slice, held between the contiguous impressions that composed our life at that time; remembrance of a particular form is but regret for a particular moment; and houses, roads, avenues are as fugitive, alas, as the years.
stops.quote_source: Swann's Way (In Search of Lost Time, Vol. 1), closing lines of 'Place-Names: The Name', trans. C. K. Scott Moncrieff (1922); en.wikisource.org
suggested_refs: The 1971 municipal deliberation renaming Illiers as Illiers-Combray
